title: Self-representation: Cheaper filings may shift institutional costs
desc: Finds rising federal self-representation without proven AI causation or improved outcomes, highlighting burdens on courts and opponents.

kps.k: The central dispute is whether cheaper legal assistance produces effective access to justice, rather than merely more legal text and court filings.
kps.d: The ABA task force and other access-oriented accounts identify three routes: direct help with rights and procedures, greater legal-aid capacity, and better court administration. They ground the need in the Legal Services Corporation’s estimate that 92% of low-income Americans’ substantial civil legal problems receive no or inadequate help. That estimate establishes unmet need, not AI effectiveness. Cohen-Sasson distinguishes access to drafting from access to remedies, while Markovic asks whether benefits survive an unequal adversarial system. Fines adds a competing baseline: for consumers unable to obtain counsel, the relevant comparison may be unsupported self-help, not an ideal lawyer.

qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: It evaluates the utility and reliability of each of these tools for individuals for whom DIY solutions are their only realistic options.
qs.a: AI, UPL, & A2J: Generative AI's Disruptions in the Delivery of Legal Services to Low-Income Individuals · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Federal filing studies document rising self-representation after public GenAI release, but do not establish that AI caused it.
kps.d: Cohen-Sasson’s overlapping analyses use approximately 2.8 million FY2008–FY2025 federal civil filings, excluding prisoner petitions and unknown case types. They report a pro se share rising from 11.33% before the cutoff to 16.94% afterward, reaching 22.30% in FY2025-Q4; the change appears as acceleration rather than an immediate jump. Shah and Levy’s broader FY2005–FY2026 dataset reports a 16.8% share in FY2025 and nearly doubled plaintiff-side pro se counts relative to FY2015–FY2022. These estimates use different samples and periods and should not be pooled. Neither design identifies a causal effect or establishes net displacement of lawyers. NCSC’s state-court contract-filing hypothesis rests on a limited convenience sample without actual AI-use or representation data.

qs.q: The exact-date rate rose from                       11.33% to 16.94% (+5.61 pp, p<0.001); FY2025-Q4 reached 22.30%.
qs.a: The New Pro Se: Generative AI and the Surge in Federal Civil Self-Representation · Academia · 2026

qs.q: 155     This Part does not establish that generative AI caused the pro se surge; the evidence is associational, though the timing, the acceleration, the robustness to controls, and the convergence of independent analyses make alternative explanations harder to sustain.
qs.a: Artificial Access to Justice: AI and the Surge in Pro Se Litigation · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Outcome evidence does not show a general improvement in litigants’ success, but the studies test different comparisons.
kps.d: Among terminated non-form cases in Cohen-Sasson’s focal categories, AI-flagged complaints have higher dismissal rates than unflagged complaints, 61.1% versus 53.6%, despite denser citations. Their win-rate difference, 6.4% versus 8.4%, is not statistically significant. Shah and Levy instead find broadly stable pre/post disposition composition and resolution speed, which they interpret as little detectable change in case quality. These findings are not directly contradictory: one compares text-flagged subsets, the other temporal cohorts, with different outcome classifications. Text flags do not verify individual AI use, citation density does not measure quality, and pending cases constrain outcome comparisons. NBC’s reported eviction success and Futurism’s costly failures illustrate possibilities, not population effects. Unchanged success rates could still accompany more favorable outcomes in absolute terms, and participation may carry independent value.

qs.q: Among terminated post-AI cases, 61.1% of AI-flagged  complaints were dismissed, against 53.6% of unflagged ones, and 47.8% ended before the  defendant answered.185 On the entry account, those gaps are best understood, at least in part, as  the visible trace of relocated screening.
qs.a: Artificial Access to Justice: AI and the Surge in Pro Se Litigation · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Cheap drafting may shift screening costs onto courts and opponents without eliminating the need for legal judgment.
kps.d: Cohen-Sasson proposes that lower drafting costs and agreeable chatbot advice admit claims that lawyers previously discouraged, moving screening into litigation. He does not identify this mechanism empirically or attribute the entire dismissal gap to it. The Ferris court separately describes an imbalance between instant fabrication and costly checking. Shah and Levy provide activity evidence: first-180-day pro se docket entries per court rose 64% on average during Q4 2022–Q2 2025 and 158% at the endpoint; entries per case also increased for represented parties. They find no corresponding slowdown in resolution. Practitioner reports of escalating fees and delays therefore support case-specific burdens, not a demonstrated nationwide congestion effect.

qs.q: 29    The Article does not contend that the whole of the gap is relocated screening.
qs.a: Artificial Access to Justice: AI and the Surge in Pro Se Litigation · Academia · 2026

qs.q: While one party can create a fake legal brief at the click of a button, the opposing party and court must parse through the case names, citations, and points of law to determine which parts, if any, are true.
qs.a: Ferris v. Amazon.com Services, LLC — Order on AI-Fabricated Citations by a Pro Se Litigant (N.D. Miss.) · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Distributional concerns extend beyond unequal tool access to AI-enabled claims against disadvantaged defendants.
kps.d: Markovic predicts that corporations and repeat players could use lower transaction costs to pursue previously uneconomic claims, increasing legal need even if defendants also adopt AI. Existing debt-collection concentration and nonresponse patterns motivate this argument; they do not measure an AI-driven boom. NCSC similarly warns about mass filing and default judgments. Digital access, language, legal literacy, trust and unequal investment may also limit effective uptake. Cohen-Sasson finds more first-observed plaintiffs among flagged complaints, weakening a purely serial-filer account, but no meaningful association with fee-waiver status. The evidence thus neither confines AI use to abusive repeat litigants nor establishes that the poorest populations disproportionately benefit.

qs.q: Legal needs could also grow exponentially as the wealthy and powerful deploy AI against low- and middle-income people in situations where hiring lawyers is currently impractical.
qs.a: Equal Justice and Generative AI · Academia · 2025

qs.q: In Oregon, 10 plaintiffs account for "more than half of all case filings and consisted entirely of third-party debt collectors, debt buyers, and national banks" and only four percent of defendants answer their case (McClendon & Kallattil, 2024).
qs.a: Is GenAI revolutionizing court filings? · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Experimental task gains support assistance, but do not establish that lay users can replace counsel.
kps.d: The GPT-4 student trial in Lawyering in the Age of Artificial Intelligence finds consistent speed gains with slight, inconsistent quality improvements. The later Vincent AI and o1-preview trial finds significant quality gains and 50%–130% productivity gains on five of six tasks, with important task exceptions and differing hallucination profiles. Nielsen and colleagues find that highlighting reduces complaint-review time by 30% without reducing measured quality; more assistance need not help more. These studies concern particular tools, outputs and student tasks, not successful rights enforcement by untrained litigants. The cognitive-reasoning articles accordingly recommend bounded uses that users can independently assess and explain. Direct-to-consumer small-claims tools lack the expert review assumed in professional assistance.

qs.q: We found that access to GPT-4 only slightly and inconsist-                        ently improved the quality of participants’ legal analysis but in-                        duced large and consistent increases in speed.
qs.a: Lawyering in the Age of Artificial Intelligence · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Our ﬁndings also show that these AI tools signiﬁcantly boost productivity in ﬁve out of six tested legal tasks, with statistically signiﬁcant gains of anywhere from 50% to 130%.
qs.a: AI-Powered Lawyering: AI Reasoning Models, Retrieval Augmented Generation, and the Future of Legal Practice · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Legal-aid evidence favors supported adoption, without yet demonstrating a reduction in unmet legal need.
kps.d: Chien and Kim surveyed 202 legal-aid professionals and gave 91 pilot participants access to paid tools, randomly assigning some additional adoption support. The intervention included conventional document automation as well as GenAI. Positive experiences, estimated time savings and continued-use intentions support the authors’ augmentation argument, but remain participant reports rather than independently measured client outcomes. Uneven organic uptake and apparently helpful support services make implementation part of the proposition. Their lawyer-directed development approach, Markovic’s proposed justice tech workers and reported successes with legal-aid guidance all preserve human assistance rather than assuming that tool availability alone supplies effective representation.

qs.q: 12 We also provided a subset of pilot participants, ran- domly chosen, with “concierge services,” including office hours and weekly emails with use cases aimed at reducing the costs of becoming familiar with the tools.
qs.a: Generative AI and Legal Aid: Results from a Field Study and 100 Use Cases to Bridge the Access to Justice Gap · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Rather than relying solely on private sector solutions, jurisdictions should train justice tech workers to counsel these communities in the responsible use of AI-based tools and verify AI-generated work product.
qs.a: Equal Justice and Generative AI · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Court-side assistance has measured promise, but this evidence supports human augmentation rather than autonomous adjudication.
kps.d: Courts of Tomorrow randomized 1,559 judges across 118 Pakistani courts. At median district exposure, AI access with targeted training corresponds to 1,848 additional annual resolutions, 6.3% above the mean, with little evidence of deterioration on observed writing, appeal and language-bias measures. Usage logs indicate research and writing assistance rather than delegated decisions; neither general safety nor transferability to US courts follows. AI Assistance for Human Review of Default Judgments reports up to 62% fewer errors and 34% time savings on document-search-intensive requirements. Its audit also identifies defects in already-granted debt judgments. These are task-specific maximum gains and a proof of concept, not evidence for replacing human review.

qs.q: We randomized 1,559 judges serving across 118 courts into one of three arms: (i) AI       access with targeted training on its use; (ii) AI access with generic training on technol-       ogy and law; or (iii) generic training without AI access.
qs.a: Courts of Tomorrow: Evidence from a Nationwide Rollout of Generative AI · Academia · 2026

qs.q: We found that AI assistance up to 62% and 34%, respectively, relative to unassisted user performance and with differences statistically       4% contained major defects that should have entirely pre- significant (p < 0.05).
qs.a: AI Assistance for Human Review of Default Judgments · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Verification is both a continuing obligation and an access problem; disagreement centers on how to make it feasible.
kps.d: Ferris applies Rule 11’s reasonable-inquiry duty to self-represented parties, while Wadsworth treats source checking as established professional practice. Critics question whether AI-specific bans, disclosures or certifications add to existing duties. Markovic instead favors enforceable certification in default-heavy proceedings, regardless of whether AI increases filings. Who Checks the Citations? argues that punishment alone may deter underserved users who lack databases and verification literacy. Practical proposals include free legal data, checking tools, court education and trained self-help staff. Checking whether an authority exists remains distinct from judging its relevance and weight; the reported detection of citation typos does not establish a general hallucination-detection rate.

qs.q: "The lie made into the rule of the world." [Franz Kafka, The Trial > 147 (1925)]  Rule 11, which applies to all parties, including pro se litigants, provides that when a paper is submitted to the court, "[a] party certifies that to the best of the person's knowledge, … formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances: …[the] legal contentions are warranted by existing law…" Fed.

qs.q: I'm not sure that AI-specific bans or certifications add much (if anything) to Rule 11.
qs.a: Lawyers' Monopoly and the Promises of AI · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Regulatory reform proposals seek to enable guided consumer help while retaining protection against unreliable services.
kps.d: Fines and Re-Regulating UPL in an Age of AI argue that unauthorized-practice restrictions can obstruct affordable personalized assistance and attorney–developer collaboration. Interoperable Legal AI separately identifies nonlawyer-ownership restrictions, jurisdictional fragmentation and corporate-focused development as scaling barriers. Proposed responses include revisiting UPL boundaries, temporary safe harbors, quality certification and regulatory sandboxes that collect evidence. These are distinct mechanisms, not established access gains. The competing concern is that legal advice delivered without accountable expertise can harm users; the proposals generally seek supervised experimentation rather than unrestricted deployment.

qs.q: Considering the potential benefit to consumers, state legislatures should re-evaluate the scope of UPL laws in order to expand assistance while still protecting consumers from negligent or fraudulent legal services.
qs.a: Re-Regulating UPL in an Age of AI · Academia · 2024

qs.q: By relaxing UPL restrictions and encouraging collaboration between attorneys and AI developers, the legal system can balance consumer protection with innovation, ensuring that AI serves as a tool to expand access to justice.
qs.a: AI, UPL, & A2J: Generative AI's Disruptions in the Delivery of Legal Services to Low-Income Individuals · Academia · 2025

kps.k: The practical agenda combines procedural redesign with evaluation of comprehension, fairness and remedies—not throughput alone.
kps.d: Cohen-Sasson proposes AI-aware forms, candid front-end guidance and liberal construction based on litigant status rather than polished prose. His predicted loss of judicial solicitude rests on doctrinal analogy, not direct evidence of judges reading AI pleadings. He would permit automated completeness checks and routing but reserve denial of a hearing to humans. Shah and Levy contemplate more extensive AI-heavy triage; judicial interviewees emphasize retaining outcome discretion. Human-centered research and controlled pilots offer a way to test these competing designs. Relevant outcomes include procedural defects, amendments, substantive remedies, user understanding and burdens on others, with longer follow-up and attention to defendants and state courts. Faster processing or lower dismissal alone cannot establish better justice.

qs.q: 254     No study yet examines how judges read AI-drafted pleadings; two adjacent literatures supply the mechanism.
qs.a: Artificial Access to Justice: AI and the Surge in Pro Se Litigation · Academia · 2026

qs.q: If lower courts are already burdened, this may even require more drastic action, as in the construction of a new lower court that triages the simplest cases mostly with AI.
qs.a: Access to Justice in the Age of AI: Evidence from U.S. Federal Courts · Academia · 2026

vlens.an:
The curated academia-and-research sources generally accept the proposition’s core distinction: cheaper AI-assisted drafting or greater filing capacity does not by itself demonstrate effective access to justice, improved litigant outcomes, or lawyer displacement. They materially develop that proposition in several ways. Large-scale federal-court studies document historically unusual growth in self-representation and docket activity while explicitly limiting their conclusions to association rather than proven GenAI causation. Complaint-level analysis finds more polished, citation-dense filings without higher per-case success and advances—but does not empirically isolate—the mechanism that screening costs migrate to judges, court staff and defendants. Other work extends the distributional analysis to repeat-player advantages, digital and verification inequalities, and the risk that cheaper claims increase legal needs for disadvantaged defendants.

The sources also add a constructive implementation agenda. Experimental studies show that AI can improve speed and, with newer tools, quality on bounded legal tasks, but those studies largely involve law students, legal-aid professionals or judges rather than autonomous lay representation. Field and court studies therefore favor augmentation: targeted training, lawyer-directed legal-aid tools, trained intermediaries, citation verification, public legal-data infrastructure and AI-assisted human court review. Regulatory scholarship adds guided consumer assistance, UPL reform and controlled sandboxes.

Material internal variation concerns emphasis rather than a clear split over the proposition. Some sources focus directly on federal filing growth and shifted institutional burdens; others redirect toward longstanding state-court dysfunction, regulatory fragmentation, consumer baselines or preservation of professional reasoning. The outcome studies also use different comparisons: AI-flagged complaints show worse dismissal trajectories, whereas broader pre/post cohorts show little detectable change in disposition composition or resolution speed. Several exploratory or bibliographic excerpts are too limited to classify. These variations do not amount to opposition, and the selected sources should not be treated as representative of academia or research as a whole.

qs.q: We do not claim to identify a causal effect of GPT-4 on pro se filing, only that the observed time series is difficult to rationalize without generative AI playing a role.
qs.a: Access to Justice in the Age of AI: Evidence from U.S. Federal Courts · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: This curated set of regulators, courts and professional bodies broadly accepts the proposition’s core distinction: cheaper AI-enabled assistance may improve access to legal information or court participation, but neither greater filing volume nor easier drafting establishes improved access-to-justice outcomes. These sources commonly ground their caution in unreliable legal outputs, the continuing need for human verification, unequal access, unauthorized-practice concerns, and the risk that courts and opponents must absorb the cost of checking AI-generated material. They also preserve the synthesis’s causal limits: the NCSC brief lacks data on actual AI use or representation, and judicial observations of increased self-represented filings are qualitative rather than proof that GenAI caused the increase. The voice materially builds on the proposition by proposing institutional responses—including monitoring filings, debt-case safeguards, more legally trained court staff, citation-verification training, AI-assisted sufficiency checks and regulatory sandboxes. Internal variation is substantial: Ferris and interviewed judges foreground burden and system capacity; bar-task-force reports emphasize conditional access benefits and responsible innovation; one Fifth Circuit commenter redirects attention to overbroad AI-specific certification; and another report explores direct-to-litigant or agentic uses without enough evidence to resolve the proposition. These positions should not be read as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: While one party can create a fake legal brief at the click of a button, the opposing party and court must parse through the case names, citations, and points of law to determine which parts, if any, are true.
qs.a: Ferris v. Amazon.com Services, LLC — Order on AI-Fabricated Citations by a Pro Se Litigant (N.D. Miss.) · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The curated market-analyst, consultancy and press sources support the proposition that easier AI-assisted self-representation can generate practical help while shifting screening and response burdens onto courts and opposing parties, without proving improved outcomes or AI causation at population level. Their common basis is reported experience rather than systematic causal evidence: both describe AI lowering barriers to producing legal material, but also show that legal judgment and verification remain necessary. Material variation lies in emphasis. Futurism foregrounds case-specific burdens—voluminous filings, increased defence work, delays and pressure on court staff—while preserving a limited role for guided AI use. NBC News presents a more balanced practical account, pairing help with procedure and jargon, including one reported eviction success, against penalties for inaccurate filings and warnings that AI cannot generally replace legal analysis. These sources therefore reinforce the synthesis’s caution but do not establish nationwide congestion, a general deterioration in case quality, or broad access-to-justice gains. Because the corpus is curated, this position characterizes only the supplied sources and should not be treated as representative of market analysts, consultancies or the press generally.

qs.q: Once a complaint is filed, attorneys told us, litigants using AI often proceed to file a steady drip of new motions and other documents, prompting the professionals on the other side of the case to pour a huge number of hours into reading and responding to the outflow of material.

elens.an: The 2015–2022 source redirects the cluster’s principal proposition from the later empirical question of whether cheaper AI-enabled filing increases federal self-representation and shifts screening or verification costs onto courts and opponents. It instead foregrounds persistent unmet legal need, presents automation and high-quality self-help as possible ways to reduce barriers, and advocates regulatory sandboxes for supervised testing. It therefore anticipates the cluster’s regulatory-experimentation strand and shares its caution that potential access gains require evaluation, but it does not examine rising self-representation, establish AI causation, measure litigant outcomes, or assess institutional cost shifting. Its claims about access benefits are prospective or attributed rather than demonstrated. This assessment concerns the supplied curated source, not the prevalence of this view across the period.

elens.an:
The 2023–2024 sources broadly support the synthesis’s principal proposition, chiefly by distinguishing inexpensive production of legal text from effective access to justice. They commonly begin from severe unmet civil legal need and treat generative AI as potentially useful for basic guidance, forms, research and legal-aid capacity. Yet they generally characterize those access benefits as predictions rather than measured improvements in remedies or litigant outcomes. Experimental evidence from this period is similarly bounded: studies of law students show substantial task-speed gains, but limited, uneven or output-specific quality effects, and therefore do not establish that untrained litigants can replace counsel.

The recurring reasons for caution are unreliable legal answers and fabricated citations, users’ limited ability to verify outputs, bias and unequal digital uptake, unauthorized-practice concerns, and the continuing need for contextual legal judgment. Several sources also anticipate the synthesis’s institutional-cost mechanism: pro se hallucination cases demonstrate case-specific burdens, while one court-focused source expressly predicts an influx of citations requiring additional court-side evaluation and verification. That source materially extends the proposition with proposals for legally trained staff, specialized verification training and amended court rules.

Material variation concerns response and emphasis rather than rejection. Access-oriented bar reports and articles are comparatively optimistic about responsible public-facing tools; experimental sources focus narrowly on augmentation and efficiency; one UPL source prioritizes regulated liberalization; a court-reform account redirects attention toward longstanding self-representation and court-process redesign; and a Fifth Circuit comment redirects toward avoiding overbroad AI certification. Bibliographic or fragmentary materials remain indeterminate. Taken together, this curated set largely supplies the conceptual risks, bounded productivity evidence and institutional-response proposals that support the later synthesis, but it does not itself establish the synthesis’s federal filing trend, AI causation, population-level outcomes or nationwide congestion effects.

elens.an:
The curated 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition’s central distinction between cheaper or faster AI-assisted legal production and effective access to justice, while materially developing the conditions and mechanisms that determine whether adoption helps or harms. Empirical and field-oriented sources find more consistent gains in speed and practitioner capacity than in legal quality or litigant outcomes; legal-aid evidence therefore favors lawyer augmentation, practical adoption support and human verification rather than autonomous substitution. Court and litigation sources reinforce the cost-shifting mechanism: inaccurate or fabricated material can be generated rapidly but requires courts and opponents to undertake disproportionately costly verification. Other sources extend the distributional analysis, arguing that lower transaction costs may advantage corporate repeat players, intensify default-heavy litigation and leave disadvantaged defendants worse off even if consumer tools become widely available.

There is material internal variation over the appropriate response. Some sources propose trained justice-tech intermediaries, certification, guided consumer tools or expertise-sensitive limits on use. Others prefer existing Rule 11 duties, controlled court pilots and hybrid human–AI models, questioning whether AI-specific bans or certifications add value. Fines uses unsupported self-help—not representation by an ideal lawyer—as the relevant baseline and supports relaxing UPL restrictions to enable guided assistance. By contrast, the interoperability and ABA-report sources redirect attention toward regulatory sandboxes, technical infrastructure and prospective court administration without directly testing the proposition’s causal or outcome claims. Exploratory and bibliographic sources remain insufficient to take a position. Thus, the period’s evidence does not establish that AI caused rising self-representation or improved justice outcomes, but it strengthens and extends the proposition by specifying adoption support, verification capacity, institutional design and unequal litigation power as decisive variables. Because these are curated sources, this synthesis describes their relationship to the proposition and does not imply prevalence across any wider group.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that cheaper AI-assisted drafting may expand court entry without demonstrated improvement in litigants’ substantive success, while shifting work to courts and opposing parties. They materially develop it in three ways. First, large observational federal-court studies document historically unusual growth in self-representation and docket activity, but consistently stop short of causal attribution; their outcome comparisons differ internally, with Cohen-Sasson finding higher dismissal among AI-flagged complaints while Shah and Levy find little detectable pre/post change in disposition composition or resolution speed. Second, qualitative practitioner and judicial accounts illustrate case-specific review costs, delay and voluminous filings, but cannot establish prevalence or nationwide congestion. Third, experimental and design-oriented sources identify responses: targeted, workflow-specific AI assistance can increase judicial output; citation-backed tools can improve human review; and verification literacy, free legal data and automated checking may make assistance safer for self-represented litigants. These extensions favor human augmentation, training and procedural redesign rather than autonomous adjudication or bans. Material variation remains: one source redirects attention to preserving lawyers’ substantive reasoning, another leaves the effects of direct-to-litigant assistance unclear, and productivity studies involving law students support bounded task assistance rather than lay replacement of counsel. Across the period, no source-level evidence establishes that GenAI caused the filing increase, generally improves remedies, or has already produced system-wide congestion.

qs.q: We do not claim to identify a causal effect of GPT-4 on pro se filing, only that the observed time series is difficult to rationalize without generative AI playing a role.
